analysis.one_liner: Taxes large investors 1-5% on each single-family home they buy, funding affordable housing programs.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in January 2024, got one committee hearing in March, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a new tax on companies and investors that buy single-family homes to rent them out. Investors owning 16-25 homes would pay 1% of each purchase price, those owning 26-100 would pay 3%, and those owning more than 100 would pay 5%. The money would go to federal affordable-housing funds, and nonprofit housing groups, land banks, community land trusts, and governments would be exempt. It also raises the minimum federal housing funding guaranteed to each state from $3 million to $7 million.
analysis.who_benefits: First-time homebuyers and renters in markets where large investors are competing for houses, because a tax on each purchase makes investor bids less attractive and frees up homes for owner-occupants. Low-income renters gain from additional funding for the Housing Trust Fund and Capital Magnet Fund, which finance affordable rental housing. Small states gain from the higher $7 million minimum allocation. Nonprofit housing groups, land banks, and community land trusts are explicitly exempt, so their ability to buy homes is untouched.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an excise tax of 1%, 3%, or 5% of the purchase price on investor purchases of single-family homes, scaled to how many homes the investor already owns (16-25, 26-100, or more than 100).
Directs 65% of the tax revenue to the Housing Trust Fund and 35% to the Capital Magnet Fund, which finance low-income rental housing and homeownership.
Raises the minimum annual Housing Trust Fund allocation for states from $3 million to $7 million, guaranteeing more funding for low-income housing in every state.

Exempts new construction, nonprofit affordable-housing groups, state and local governments, public housing authorities, land banks, and community land trusts, so the tax targets investor flipping and accumulation, not homebuilding.

analysis.who_pays: Corporate and large individual investors in single-family rental housing, including big institutional landlords, who would pay a 1-5% tax on every home they buy. Some of that cost could be passed on through rents, and sellers of homes to investors could see somewhat lower demand for their properties.

drawbacks.text: The tax is levied only on purchases, so it may not push large investors to sell the estimated millions of homes they already own; investors could also shift to buying through structures the aggregation rules do not reach.
Investors may pass part of the tax to renters through higher rents, since most investor-owned homes are rentals.

A 1% rate for smaller investors (16-25 homes) taxes small landlords along with corporate buyers, and defining ownership thresholds in a market this varied will inevitably draw lines someone thinks are wrong.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: any tax that makes it costlier for large investors to outbid families for starter homes, while funding affordable housing directly, targets a widely felt affordability problem. The design limitations are honest ones — it taxes new purchases rather than forcing existing investor-owned homes onto the market, and it may capture small landlords as well as giants — but the exemptions for nonprofits and land banks show the targeting was thought through. On balance a plainly pro-homebuyer, pro-renter bill whose main cost falls on concentrated investor interests.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it died without a floor vote when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Jack Reed and six Democratic colleagues introduced the bill on January 25, 2024, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee.

The only action after referral was a Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee hearing on March 12, 2024 (S.Hrg. 118-548); the Finance Committee, which had jurisdiction, never marked up or reported the bill.
With no committee action and no floor vote in either chamber, the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large single-family rental investors are better off, since no tax will be imposed on their home purchases; first-time homebuyers and renters gain nothing because the housing-fund money never materialized.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large investors who buy homes to rent

for.name: Sen. Jack Reed
for.role: Sponsor, U.S. Senator from Rhode Island
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized six Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: Senate Democratic cosponsors (Smith, Gillibrand, Blumenthal, Klobuchar, Fetterman, Baldwin)
Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
for.what_they_did: Held hearings (S.Hrg. 118-548) in March 2024, the only committee activity connected to the bill.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over the bill's tax provisions
against.what_they_did: Never marked up, reported, or scheduled the bill after its January 2024 referral, letting it sit until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill received no committee or floor action in the Republican-led or divided 118th Congress.

industries.industry: Institutional and large investors in single-family rental homes (corporate landlords, funds, home-flippers)
industries.note: They would pay 1-5% of the price on every single-family home they buy, directly raising the cost of the buy-to-rent strategy that has priced many families out of starter homes. Their gain from the bill dying is keeping that cost off the books.

industries.industry: Real estate brokerage and home-sale market participants serving investor buyers
industries.note: A tax on investor purchases could reduce transaction volume in hot markets where investors are heavy buyers, but could also shift sales toward owner-occupants. Agents selling to families would see little change.

industries.industry: Affordable housing nonprofits, land banks, and community land trusts
industries.note: They are exempt from the tax and benefit from the added Housing Trust Fund and Capital Magnet Fund revenue, giving them an edge over taxed investors in acquiring homes.
